Botanical leaves rendered against a silver-white ground, the composition with the stillness of a winter morning. This scroll was hung in its traditional format and placed within a natural wood frame to protect it.

The Hakone Open Air Museum sits in the mountains of Kanagawa Prefecture, surrounded by sculpture gardens with views of Fuji. In winter, the combination of cold mountain air, mist, and monumental sculpture creates an atmosphere of rare, meditative beauty. This scroll came home from that day in January 2026.

Look closely at the pin holding the scroll’s string at the top. It is a small deity pin given freely by a monk at Honsenji Temple in Shinagawa, Tokyo — on New Year’s Eve 2025, at the Joya no Kane ceremony, folded inside a tiny piece of paper. Honsenji is the temple of Bishamonten on the Tokai Shichifukujin pilgrimage route — the god of war, treasure, and protection, one of Japan’s Seven Lucky Gods.

Joya no Kane is one of Japan’s most ancient Buddhist rituals: the temple bell is rung 108 times at midnight, once for each of the worldly desires that accumulate over the year. Honsenji’s giant bell has its own extraordinary history — it was taken out of Japan, found in Switzerland, and returned to the temple in 1930. At midnight, as the bell rang in the new year, this small deity was acquired at the temple. It now holds up the scroll.
